Title: Standard revenue case — straightforward sale with single performance obligation

Opening / definition
A “standard revenue case” describes a straightforward sales contract in which a seller transfers goods or a service that gives rise to a single performance obligation satisfied at a point in time. These transactions have no material complications such as variable consideration, significant financing components, separate warranties or post-delivery obligations. Getting these cases right is important because they are common, form the baseline for more complex situations and usually require clear, efficient accounting and disclosure (ASC 606, IFRS 15; Deloitte Revenue Guidance).

The five‑step model — brief overview
ASC 606 and IFRS 15 require the same five‑step approach to revenue recognition:
1) Identify the contract with the customer — confirm enforceable rights/obligations and collectibility (ASC 606, IFRS 15).
2) Identify the performance obligations — determine distinct promised goods or services; a “standard” case has one (transfer of goods) (ASC 606, IFRS 15).
3) Determine the transaction price — the amount the entity expects in exchange, considering any discounts or adjustments.
4) Allocate the transaction price — assign the price to each performance obligation; with a single obligation allocation equals the full price.
5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies the performance obligation — at a point in time for typical goods sales (ASC 606, IFRS 15; PwC Revenue Guidance).

Worked example — 100 widgets sold to Customer A
Facts
- Company sells 100 identical widgets to Customer A for a total contract price of $10,000.
- Delivery occurs June 30; cash is received at delivery.
- No returns, no installation services, no significant financing, no continuing obligations.
- Inventory cost = $6,000.

Apply the five steps
1) Identify the contract: There is an enforceable contract with Customer A and collectibility is not in question (step 1 satisfied) (ASC 606, IFRS 15).
2) Identify performance obligation(s): The contract promises transfer of goods only. The widgets are a single, distinct performance obligation (step 2).
3) Determine the transaction price: The fixed price is $10,000; there is no variable consideration or financing component (step 3).
4) Allocate the transaction price: Only one performance obligation exists, so allocation = $10,000 (step 4).
5) Recognize revenue: The obligation is satisfied when control of the widgets transfers to Customer A — delivery on June 30. Revenue recognized on June 30 in the amount of $10,000 (step 5).

Journal entries at delivery/receipt (June 30)
- To record receipt of cash and revenue:
  Debit Cash $10,000
  Credit Revenue $10,000

- To record cost of goods sold and reduce inventory (assuming cost = $6,000):
  Debit Cost of Goods Sold $6,000
  Credit Inventory $6,000

Balance sheet and profit impact
- Immediately after recognition, the income statement shows Revenue $10,000 and COGS $6,000 (Gross profit $4,000).
- Cash (or Accounts Receivable if billed) increases by $10,000; Inventory decreases by $6,000. No contract asset/liability remains because performance and collection occurred simultaneously.

Note on tax vs accounting timing
Tax rules may differ from accounting recognition dates. In many jurisdictions, tax follows revenue recognition for financial reporting; in others, tax may use invoice/billing or cash basis rules. Consider deferred tax implications when timing differs.

Common pitfalls & practical checks
1) Return rights: Even modest return rights can create variable consideration or require expected returns accounting. Confirm explicit return clauses and historical return rates (ASC 606; KPMG guidance).
2) Consignment arrangements: If goods are on consignment, control hasn’t transferred on delivery to a third party — revenue recognition is deferred until performance criteria are met (ASC 606, IFRS 15).
3) Principal vs agent: If the entity arranges sales for a third party, assess whether it controls the goods or is an agent; principal accounts for gross revenue, agent recognizes net fee (ASC 606; Deloitte Roadmap).
4) Point in time vs over time: Confirm indicators of transfer of control (right to payment, physical possession, transfer of significant risks/rewards, acceptance) to justify point‑in‑time recognition (PwC/EY summaries).
5) Billing vs recognition: Billing or cash receipt doesn’t automatically equal revenue recognition. Revenue follows satisfaction of performance obligations, not invoicing (ASC 606).
6) Hidden services or obligations: Check for implicit post‑delivery obligations (e.g., installation, training, extended support) that could create separate or additional obligations.
7) Significant financing: If payment timing materially differs from transfer of control, evaluate whether a significant financing component exists and adjust the transaction price.
8) Contract modifications: Late changes in price/quantity can affect allocation and timing — document and test modifications against the standard.

Disclosures and presentation
For a standard sale, disclosures are typically straightforward: recognize the nature of goods sold, timing of revenue recognition (point in time), and the transaction price for major categories (ASC 606, IFRS 15). Entities should present revenue gross or net depending on principal vs agent assessment, and disclose significant judgments (e.g., determination of control, return policies). Quantitative disclosure for individual simple transactions is not required, but policies and methods should be explained in the revenue note (Deloitte, PwC guidance).

Short checklist / takeaway
1) Is there a valid contract and collectibility? 2) Is there only one distinct performance obligation? 3) Is the transaction price fixed and simple? 4) Does control transfer at a point in time? 5) Any returns, consignment, or agent/principal issues? 6) Are journal entries and disclosures consistent with the answers above?

If the answers are all yes/clear, treat the transaction as a standard revenue case: recognize revenue when control transfers and record COGS for the associated inventory cost.

Draft Title: Recognizing Revenue in a Standard Case (ASC 606 / IFRS 15) — Practical Guide

Opening: what a “standard revenue case” means and why ASC 606/IFRS 15 matters (≈120 words)

This guide focuses on common, “standard” revenue transactions — straightforward product sales, subscription or service arrangements, and simple bundled offers — and shows how to apply the five-step revenue-recognition model used by ASC 606 and IFRS 15. The objective of the standards is to depict the transfer of promised goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled. For most routine commercial transactions this leads to either point-in-time or over-time recognition with predictable journal entries. This note is practical, example-driven, and intended as a refresher for accounting professionals and finance managers. It is not legal or tax advice; consult advisers for jurisdiction-specific treatment. (See FASB ASC 606; IFRS 15.)

The five-step model (≈180 words)

1) Identify the contract with a customer — an agreement creating enforceable rights and obligations. Assess collectibility and whether the contract has commercial substance.
2) Identify the performance obligations (POs) — promises to transfer distinct goods or services.
3) Determine the transaction price — the amount expected, including estimates of variable consideration, adjusted for significant financing components, noncash consideration, and consideration payable to a customer.
4) Allocate the transaction price to each PO based on their relative standalone selling prices (SSPs).
5) Recognize revenue when (or as) each PO is satisfied — i.e., when control of the good or service transfers to the customer (point in time) or over time if criteria are met (progress toward satisfaction).

These steps and their application are summarized in ASC 606 and IFRS 15; professional guidance from the Big Four provides useful implementation examples (PwC, Deloitte, EY, KPMG).

Three worked examples with journal entries (≈450 words)

1) Simple product sale — immediate recognition (point in time)

Scenario: On 15 March, Company A sells inventory for $10,000 cash. The inventory cost is $6,000. There is a clear transfer of control at delivery.

Journal entries (15 March)
- Receipt of cash and revenue recognition:
  Dr Cash 10,000
  Cr Sales revenue 10,000

- Remove inventory and recognize cost of goods sold:
  Dr Cost of goods sold 6,000
  Cr Inventory 6,000

Why: Control transfers at delivery, consideration is fixed and collectible; apply step 5 at a point in time. (See indicators of control such as present right to payment, transfer of legal title, physical possession.)

2) Subscription/service contract — performance over time (ratable recognition)

Scenario: On 1 Jan, Company B (SaaS) receives $1,200 cash for a 12-month subscription starting that day. There are no other promised goods or variable terms.

Journal entries
- On contract inception (1 Jan):
  Dr Cash 1,200
  Cr Deferred revenue (contract liability) 1,200

- Monthly recognition (end of each month):
  Dr Deferred revenue 100
  Cr Service revenue 100

Why: The entity’s obligation is to provide access to service over time. Recognition is based on time-elapsed (or another appropriate measure of progress) because the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits.

3) Bundled goods + service — allocate using standalone selling prices

Scenario: On 1 Apr, Company C sells a device plus a 12-month support service for a total price of $2,000, paid upfront. The company’s standalone selling prices are: device $1,500; service $600 (sum = $2,100). Device cost = $900.

Allocation:
- Device share = 1,500/2,100 = 71.4286 → allocated price = 2,000 × 0.714286 = 1,428.57
- Service share = 600/2,100 = 28.5714 → allocated price = 571.43 (to be recognized over 12 months ≈ 47.62/month)

Journal entries
- On payment/contract date (1 Apr):
  Dr Cash 2,000
  Cr Contract liability 2,000

- At delivery (control transfers — recognize device revenue immediately):
  Dr Contract liability 1,428.57
  Cr Sales revenue — device 1,428.57

  Dr Cost of goods sold 900
  Cr Inventory 900

- Monthly service recognition (end of month):
  Dr Contract liability 47.62
  Cr Service revenue 47.62

Note rounding considerations when allocating; disclose the basis for SSPs and rounding policies.

Practical considerations (≈170 words)

Point in time vs. over time: Revenue is recognized over time when (a) the customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits, (b) the seller’s performance creates/enhances an asset the customer controls as it is created, or (c) the seller’s performance does not create an asset with an alternative use and the seller has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date (ASC 606/IFRS 15 criteria). Otherwise recognize at the point control transfers.

Variable consideration: Constrain estimates (expected value or most likely amount) to avoid significant reversals. Examples include refunds, rebates, and performance bonuses. Document judgement and any expected reversals.

Contract modifications: Treat as a separate contract only if it adds distinct goods/services and additional consideration consistent with standalone prices; otherwise treat as modification to existing contract and reallocate.

Impairment of receivables vs revenue: Loss allowances (credit impairment) affect receivables, not revenue recognition, unless collectibility was not assessed as probable at contract inception (that could affect whether a contract is in-scope).

Disclosures (concise)

For standard cases disclose: the accounting policy for revenue recognition, significant judgments (e.g., determining SSPs, variable consideration estimates, timing of transfer), significant contract balances (contract liabilities, receivables), and revenue disaggregated by type or timing. Include reconciliations of opening and closing contract liabilities where material. (See ASC 606 / IFRS 15 disclosure requirements and SEC guidance for public companies.)

Common pitfalls & quick checklist (≈70 words)

Checklist for reviewers:
- Have all performance obligations been identified and are any incorrectly aggregated or split?
- Is transaction price properly estimated (variable consideration constrained)?
- Are SSPs supportable and consistently applied for allocation?
- Was a significant financing component overlooked?
- Is the chosen measure of progress appropriate and consistently applied?
- Are contract modifications handled and documented?

References (authoritative)

- FASB ASC 606 overview and guidance: https://asc.fasb.org
- IFRS 15 (IFRS Foundation): https://www.ifrs.org/standards/ifrs-15-revenue-from-contracts-with-customers/
- PwC: Practical Guide to Revenue Recognition (Revenue from Contracts with Customers)
- Deloitte: Roadmap — Revenue from Contracts with Customers
- SEC staff summaries/guidance on revenue recognition

Notes: This draft focuses on standard cases and rounded simple numbers. Jurisdiction-specific tax or regulatory outcomes are out of scope and should be reviewed with legal/tax advisers. Flag any areas you want expanded or additional illustrative journal entries.

Title: Standard‑Revenue Case: How to Recognize, Report, and Model Revenue under the Standard Case

Introduction: what is a standard‑revenue case and why it matters

A “standard‑revenue case” is a straightforward customer contract in which a single performance obligation (PO) exists and the consideration is fixed or effectively fixed, such that revenue recognition follows the ordinary, non‑complex application of ASC 606 / IFRS 15. Typical examples: a 12‑month SaaS subscription with a fixed fee, a single product sale with standard delivery, or a plain‑vanilla service contract where the seller’s promise is to provide a single, well‑defined good or service.

Why it matters: standard cases make up most recurring revenue streams and are often presented in management reporting and forecasts. Getting them right improves comparability, reduces audit friction, and simplifies modeling.

Assumptions for this article: USD reporting, principles equally applicable under ASC 606 and IFRS 15 unless noted. Example uses a SaaS subscription contract.

The five‑step model in brief

Both ASC 606 and IFRS 15 use the same five‑step model: 1) Identify the contract(s) with a customer; 2) Identify the performance obligation(s); 3) Determine the transaction price; 4) Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligation(s); 5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation (i.e., when control transfers).

For a standard case these steps typically map directly: one contract, one PO, transaction price is the contract price (less immaterial taxes), allocation is trivial, and revenue is recognized over time or at a point in time depending on control transfer tests.

Point in time vs over time: decision rules (decision tree)

Key question: does the seller satisfy the PO over time or at a point in time? Use the following hierarchy (ASC 606 / IFRS 15):

ASCII decision tree:
If (customer receives and consumes benefits as seller performs) OR (seller’s performance creates/enhances an asset the customer controls) OR (seller has no alternative use to seller AND right to payment for performance completed to date) → recognize over time. Else → recognize at point in time.

Practical point: for services (e.g., SaaS), over‑time recognition is common (customer receives benefit continuously). For discrete goods delivered and transferred at delivery, point in time usually applies.

Measurement & timing — what to model

Transaction price: usually the fixed contract consideration. Exclude sales taxes, reimbursements, and amounts collected on behalf of third parties. Consider whether variable consideration exists (discounts, usage, refunds). If variable consideration is immaterial or constrained, treat the price as fixed.

Allocation: with a single PO allocation is trivial — the whole transaction price. With multiple POs you’d allocate by stand‑alone selling price (not the focus here).

Progress measurement (for over‑time recognition): choose output (e.g., milestones, hours delivered, months elapsed) or input (cost‑to‑cost). Common for SaaS: straight‑line (time elapsed / contract term) as output method because benefit to customer is time‑based.

Contract assets/liabilities: if cash received before satisfaction of PO, record contract liability (deferred revenue). If revenue recognized before invoicing or billing, record contract asset.

Contract costs: incremental costs of obtaining a contract (e.g., sales commissions) may be capitalized and amortized; costs to fulfil may be expensed unless they meet capitalization criteria. Document judgments.

Worked example: step‑by‑step (SaaS subscription)

Facts and assumptions
- Contract: 12‑month SaaS subscription starting 1 Jan 2025
- Contract price: $120,000, invoiced and paid in full on signing (1 Jan 2025)
- No variable consideration, no significant financing (payment in full at inception but for simplicity assume no material financing component), no additional POs
- The service transfers to the customer over time (continuous access), measured on a time‑elapsed (straight‑line) basis
- Expected costs to provide service: $60,000 evenly incurred over term

Recognition logic
- Transaction price = $120,000
- Single PO → allocate full $120,000
- Over‑time recognition using output method (time elapsed): $120,000 / 12 months = $10,000 per month

Journal entries (selected)
1) At contract inception / cash receipt (1 Jan 2025)
   Dr Cash $120,000
   Cr Contract liability — Deferred revenue $120,000
   Rationale: cash received in advance of performance

2) Monthly revenue recognition (e.g., end of Jan 2025)
   Dr Contract liability — Deferred revenue $10,000
   Cr Revenue — Subscription service $10,000

3) Monthly cost recognition (assuming costs incurred monthly $5,000)
   Dr Cost of services $5,000
   Cr Cash / Payables $5,000

Notes: if company recognizes revenue before invoicing, entry would be Dr Contract asset / Receivable; Cr Revenue, and cash receipt reduces the receivable or liability accordingly.

Period table (sample months 1–4 shown; full 12‑month pattern continues)

Period, Revenue recognized, Cumulative revenue, Contract liability (opening → closing), Cash receipts
Jan‑25: $10,000, $10,000, $120,000 → $110,000, $120,000 (receipt at inception)
Feb‑25: $10,000, $20,000, $110,000 → $100,000, $120,000
Mar‑25: $10,000, $30,000, $100,000 → $90,000, $120,000
Apr‑25: $10,000, $40,000, $90,000 → $80,000, $120,000
... continue until Dec‑25 where cumulative revenue $120,000 and contract liability $0.

(If the company billed monthly instead, cash receipts would match recognized revenue and contract liability movements would differ.)

CSV snippet (downloadable by copy/paste to a .csv file)
Period,Revenue,CumulativeRevenue,ContractLiabilityOpening,ContractLiabilityClosing,CashReceipt
Jan-25,10000,10000,120000,110000,120000
Feb-25,10000,20000,110000,100000,0
Mar-25,10000,30000,100000,90000,0
Apr-25,10000,40000,90000,80000,0
... , , , , , 

Model formula examples (spreadsheet)
- Monthly revenue = TransactionPrice / TermMonths
- CumulativeRevenue_t = CumulativeRevenue_{t-1} + MonthlyRevenue
- ContractLiabilityClosing_t = ContractLiabilityOpening_t - MonthlyRevenue + CashReceived_t
- Input method %complete = CostsIncurredToDate / TotalExpectedCosts
- Revenue recognized (input) = %complete * TotalTransactionPrice - RevenueRecognizedToDate

Modeling and disclosure tips

Spreadsheet layout (simple): columns for Period, Days in Period, %Elapsed, RevenueRecognized, CumulativeRevenue, ContractLiabilityOpening, CashReceived, ContractLiabilityClosing, CostsIncurred, CumulativeCosts, %Complete (if input method), Notes.

Formulas: anchor the transaction price and expected costs in separate cells and reference them to avoid hard‑coded numbers. Use row‑replicate formulas for period calculations so changes propagate.

Sensitivity: test scenarios for variable consideration, cancellations, or change in term (prorate remaining revenue). Model the effect of a contract modification — if it adds a distinct service, treat as a new contract; otherwise account for as a modification (prospective or cumulative catch‑up depending on guidance).

Presentation: present deferred revenue (contract liability) on the balance sheet and disclose revenue recognized by major categories, timing of transfer (point in time vs over time), significant judgments, and methods used to measure progress. Reconcile opening and closing contract balances in notes.

Common pitfalls & compliance checklist

Checklist for finance teams / auditors:
- Have you identified all POs? Single PO or multiple?
- Have you tested point‑in‑time vs over‑time criteria and documented rationale? (Use decision tree)
- Is variable consideration present? If yes, have you applied constraint and estimation methods?
- Are progress measurement methods consistent, supportable, and documented (input vs output)?
- Have you considered significant financing components for long‑term prepayments?
- Are incremental contract costs accounted for and amortized appropriately?
- Are contract assets/liabilities reconciliations prepared and consistent with cash flows and revenue recognized?
- Are disclosures complete: methods, judgments, remaining performance obligations, contract balances?

Common errors: recognizing revenue at invoicing rather than performance, failing to capture incremental costs to obtain contracts, misapplying input/output methods, inadequate support for timing judgments.

Conclusion and further reading

Standard‑revenue cases are often straightforward but require disciplined application of the five‑step model, careful documentation of timing judgments, and clear modeling of contract balances. For recurring SaaS and subscription contracts, straight‑line over the term is frequently appropriate but should be justified and stress‑tested.

Authoritative links and further reading
1) IFRS Foundation — IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers (overview): https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ifrs-15-revenue-from-contracts-with-customers/

Recognizing a “Standard” Revenue Transaction (ASC 606 / IFRS 15): A Practical Guide

High-level overview
The five-step revenue model (ASC 606 / IFRS 15) is straightforward in concept and should be applied consistently: 1) Identify the contract with a customer; 2) Identify the performance obligations in the contract; 3) Determine the transaction price; 4) Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations; 5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies each performance obligation (i.e., when control transfers) (FASB ASC 606; IFRS 15).

What I mean by a “standard‑revenue case”
A standard case for this guide is: a single-good or single-service sale with one performance obligation, no variable consideration, no significant financing component, and no material post‑delivery obligations (e.g., extended service contracts). This is the typical retail or one-off supply-of-goods sale where control passes at a point in time.

Step-by-step application to the standard case
1) Identify the contract: Confirm there is a contract that creates enforceable rights and obligations and has commercial substance. Check payment terms and collectibility is probable (ASC 606 / IFRS 15).
2) Identify the performance obligation(s): For a single good sold with no bundled services and no promised future obligations, there is one distinct performance obligation.
3) Determine the transaction price: If the price is fixed (e.g., $10,000) and there are no discounts, returns, incentives, or variable consideration, the transaction price equals the agreed amount.
4) Allocate the transaction price: With one performance obligation, the full transaction price is allocated to that obligation.
5) Recognize revenue: Determine when control transfers. For goods sold and delivered at a point in time, revenue is recognized at the moment of delivery (or earlier/later only if control transfers at a different time).

Boxed numeric example (standard goods sale)
------------------------------------------
Facts: Seller sells goods to Customer for $10,000. Seller’s cost of goods sold (COGS) = $6,000. Customer paid $10,000 in cash before delivery. Delivery and legal title transfer to Customer on Day 10; no returns, warranties beyond assurance, or other obligations.

Accounting treatment (illustrative):
- Day 0 (cash received before delivery):
  Debit Cash 10,000
  Credit Contract liability (Deferred revenue) 10,000

- Day 10 (on delivery — control transfers):
  Debit Contract liability (Deferred revenue) 10,000
  Credit Revenue 10,000

  Debit Cost of goods sold 6,000
  Credit Inventory 6,000

Notes: If payment is received at the point of delivery instead of before delivery, the typical single entry at delivery is Debit Cash 10,000 / Credit Revenue 10,000 (and the COGS / inventory entry simultaneously). If delivery and payment occur together, no contract liability arises. These journal entries are illustrative only and should be adapted to an entity’s chart of accounts and policies.

Brief ASC 606 vs IFRS 15 comparison (practical)
- The model is converged: both standards use the same five-step framework and produce the same outcome in a standard case (FASB ASC 606; IFRS 15).
- Practical phrasing differences rarely change application here. For example, both require assessing collectibility and enforceability; neither will change the timing of revenue recognition for a simple sale with transfer of control at delivery.

Checklist — what to confirm in the contract (3–6 quick items)
- Contract existence with enforceable rights and obligations; collection of consideration is probable.
- Payment terms and timing (prepayment, at delivery, or credit) and any financing component.
- Return/cancellation and refund terms that could introduce variable consideration.
- Whether any additional promises (installation, post‑sale service, warranties beyond assurance) create separate obligations.

Signs this case is NOT standard
- Variable consideration (rebates, performance bonuses, significant returns) requiring estimation and constraint.
- Multiple promised goods/services or bundled arrangements needing allocation.
- Principal versus agent considerations (are we the principal in the transaction?).
- Consignment arrangements, significant financing components, or obligations that extend materially after delivery.

Common practitioner pitfalls
- Recognizing revenue on invoicing rather than on transfer of control.
- Failing to record a contract liability when payment precedes transfer of control.
- Overlooking return or refund rights that create variable consideration.
- Misclassifying promises bundled with goods (e.g., installation considered a separate obligation when it is not).

Internal controls and disclosure implications (brief)
Controls: Ensure contracts are reviewed by finance for key terms (payment timing, returns, warranties), maintain a checklist for revenue recognition triggers, and reconcile contract liabilities and receivables regularly. Segregation of duties around contract setup, billing, and revenue posting reduces errors.
Disclosures: Even in simple cases, ASC 606 and IFRS 15 require disclosure of the nature, amount, timing, and judgments made in recognizing revenue (e.g., significant payment terms, performance obligations). For more complex portfolios, more detailed quantitative and qualitative disclosures are required (ASC 606; IFRS 15).

Sources
- FASB ASC Topic 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (overview materials).
- IFRS 15, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (IASB).
- PwC, Revenue from Contracts with Customers: Practical guides and illustrative examples.

Compliance note
This guidance is operational and illustrative. It is not tax or legal advice. Journal entries are examples and should be tailored to your entity’s chart of accounts, policies, and facts-and-circumstances.

Summary:
This practical explainer covers how to apply the five‑step ASC 606 / IFRS 15 model for straightforward sales — single contract, single performance obligation, no significant financing or variable consideration, and no major post‑sale obligations. It gives a short, realistic numeric example with journal entries (sale on delivery and advance payment cases), highlights indicators that control has transferred, calls out common pitfalls, and ends with a concise month‑end checklist and references.

Five‑step recognition process (brief):
1) Identify the contract with the customer — is there enforceable rights/obligations and commercial substance? 
2) Identify the performance obligations — what distinct goods or services are promised? For a standard sale this is typically a single obligation to transfer the goods or to perform a one‑off service. 
3) Determine the transaction price — normally the agreed fixed amount (note: exclude sales taxes). Consider whether any price concessions, discounts, or variable consideration exist. 
4) Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations — for a single obligation this step is trivial. 
5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies the performance obligation — for standard goods or single‑performance services this will usually be at a point in time (when control transfers) or upon completion of the service.

Practical indicators that control has transferred (useful for point‑in‑time cases):
- Legal title has passed to the customer.
- Physical possession has transferred.
- The customer has accepted the asset or the company has no remaining significant obligations.
- The customer bears significant risks and rewards of ownership.
- The customer has the present right to use and obtain substantially all of the remaining benefits.
(ASC 606/IFRS 15 emphasize control rather than risks-and-rewards only — consider all indicators together.)

Measurement and pricing notes:
- Transaction price is typically the fixed agreed amount. Exclude taxes collected on behalf of taxing authorities. 
- If the contract includes variable consideration (returns, rebates, discounts), estimate and constrain variable amounts per ASC 606/IFRS 15.
- Determine whether quoted prices are tax‑inclusive; report revenue net of sales taxes and VAT (i.e., the consideration that the entity expects to be entitled to).

Worked example (single sale of goods — clear numeric entries)
Facts:
- Company sells 100 units of Product X, total contract price $10,000.
- Cost of goods sold (COGS) for the 100 units: $6,000.
- Shipping term: FOB shipping point — control transfers when goods leave the seller's dock.
- No significant returns expected beyond normal warranty; assume an expected return rate of 2% for illustration.

A. Sale on delivery / payment at delivery (performance at point in time)
At shipment/delivery (control transfers):
- Debit Cash (or Accounts Receivable) $10,000
- Credit Sales Revenue $10,000
- Debit Cost of Goods Sold $6,000
- Credit Inventory $6,000
Rationale: revenue recognized at the point when control transfers (shipment under FOB shipping point).

B. Payment received in advance (cash collected before delivery)
At cash receipt (before performance):
- Debit Cash $10,000
- Credit Contract Liability — Deferred Revenue $10,000
On shipment/delivery (when performance obligation satisfied):
- Debit Contract Liability — Deferred Revenue $10,000
- Credit Sales Revenue $10,000
- Debit Cost of Goods Sold $6,000
- Credit Inventory $6,000
Rationale: cash receipt does not create revenue until the performance obligation is satisfied; until then it's a contract liability.

C. Estimating returns (simple illustration)
Assumptions: expected returns = 2% of the selling price = $200; expected cost of returns = 2% * $6,000 = $120.
At recognition (conservative approach consistent with ASC 606):
- Debit Cash/AR $10,000
- Credit Sales Revenue $9,800
- Credit Refund Liability $200
- Debit Cost of Goods Sold $5,880 (expected non‑returned COGS: $6,000 * 98/100)
- Credit Inventory $5,880
- Debit Inventory — Recoverable from Returns $120
- Credit Inventory $120
When returns occur, use the refund liability and the recoverable‑inventory asset to reverse revenue and reinstate inventory cost.

D. Warranty considerations (high level)
- Assurance‑type warranty (expected defect correction under law/contract): account for as a liability (warranty expense recognized when product sold) and disclose the measurement basis. 
- Service‑type warranty (optional extended warranty sold separately): treat as a separate performance obligation and allocate part of the transaction price to it; recognize revenue over the warranty service period.

Common pitfalls (practical):
- Treating cash receipt as revenue recognition rather than evaluating whether the performance obligation is satisfied. 
- Ignoring bundled goods/services: failure to separate distinct performance obligations can misstate timing and amount of revenue. 
- Mishandling returns and variable consideration — not estimating or constraining expected returns. 
- Misclassifying warranties (assurance vs service) — accounting treatment differs. 
- Overlooking financing components when payment timing is significantly different from performance (not common in standard, short‑term sales). 
- Incorrect recognition of tax‑inclusive prices as revenue when tax should be excluded.

- Is there a contract and a clearly identified customer? 
- What exactly did we promise? Are there multiple distinct performance obligations?
- What is the transaction price? Any discounts/variable consideration to estimate? Sales tax excluded?
- Has control transferred? If not, record/maintain contract liability (deferred revenue).
- If cash received in advance, is there an appropriate contract liability on the ledger?
- Are returns and warranties estimated and recorded appropriately? 
- Have journal entries for revenue/COGS been posted and reconciled to inventory movements and invoices?
- Are required disclosures being prepared (see references)?

Purpose and scope
This short explainer shows how to apply the five-step revenue-recognition model to a standard (uncomplicated) sale: a single contract for a promised good or service with a fixed price, no significant variable consideration, and no multiple performance obligations. It covers ASC 606 (US GAAP) and IFRS 15 (substantially converged for this scenario) and is aimed at finance managers, accountants, and startup CFOs.

What is a “standard” revenue case?
A standard case typically has all of the following: a single promised good or service (one performance obligation), a determinable (fixed or effectively fixed) transaction price, no meaningful variable consideration, no significant financing component, and no bundled deliverables or licensing complexity. If any of those elements change, the accounting may become more complex.

The five-step model applied to the standard case
1) Identify the contract with the customer
- There must be enforceable rights and obligations and commercial substance. Written or oral contracts are acceptable if they meet the criteria in ASC 606/IFRS 15. (See FASB ASC 606; IFRS 15.)

2) Identify the performance obligations in the contract
- In a standard sale, there is one performance obligation: deliver the promised good or perform the promised service. No allocation across deliverables is needed.

3) Determine the transaction price
- The transaction price is the amount the entity expects to be entitled to in exchange for transferring the promised good/service. For standard cases this is the fixed sales price. Consider discounts, rebates, and whether sales taxes should be excluded (sales taxes collected on behalf of tax authorities are not revenue). Assess whether any financing component is significant — commonly not for short-term sales. (ASC 606 / IFRS 15)

4) Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations
- With a single performance obligation, allocation is trivial: the whole transaction price maps to that obligation.

5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the performance obligation is satisfied
- For most goods the obligation is satisfied at a point in time — when control transfers to the customer (typically on delivery or when the buyer takes physical possession, depending on shipping terms). For services, recognition may be over time if the criteria are met; otherwise it is point-in-time. (ASC 606/IFRS 15 set out the over-time criteria.)

Indicators that control has transferred (examples)
- Legal title has passed.
- Customer has physical possession of the good.
- Significant risks and rewards of ownership have transferred.
- Customer has accepted the asset under the contract terms.
- Customer can direct the use of, and obtain substantially all remaining benefits from, the asset.
No single indicator is conclusive; use judgment and consider the contract facts and customary trade terms (e.g., FOB shipping point vs FOB destination).

Worked example (short)
Facts: Company A sells 1 unit of Product X to Customer B for $10,000. Shipping terms: FOB destination (control transfers on delivery). Inventory cost to Company A: $6,000. No sales taxes for simplicity.

Scenario A — Sale on delivery and cash received immediately
- At delivery (control transferred), record the sale and cost of goods sold:
  Dr Cash 10,000
  Cr Revenue 10,000
  Dr Cost of Goods Sold 6,000
  Cr Inventory 6,000
(If sales tax applies, it is recorded separately as a liability, not revenue.)

Scenario B — Sale on delivery but invoiced (payment later)
  Dr Accounts Receivable 10,000
  Cr Revenue 10,000
  Dr Cost of Goods Sold 6,000
  Cr Inventory 6,000
When cash is collected later:
  Dr Cash 10,000
  Cr Accounts Receivable 10,000

If the invoice included sales tax (e.g., 8% = $800 on top of price), the journal at invoice would be:
  Dr Accounts Receivable 10,800
  Cr Revenue 10,000
  Cr Sales Tax Payable 800
(Revenue is recorded net of sales tax because the tax is a liability collected on behalf of the authority.)

Brief note on over-time vs point-in-time
Services are often recognized over time when one of the following is met: (a) the customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits as the entity performs; (b) the entity’s performance creates (or enhances) an asset the customer controls as it is created; or (c) the entity’s performance doesn’t create an asset with an alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date. If none apply, recognize at a point in time when control transfers. (ASC 606/IFRS 15 criteria)

Common pitfalls and FAQs
- When does a simple contract become complex? If there are multiple deliverables, licensing, significant variable consideration (rebates, refunds, performance bonuses), significant financing components, or principal vs. agent questions, you need more detailed analysis and possibly allocation of price to separate obligations.
- Distinguishing point-in-time vs. over-time: always map the facts (who controls the asset as it is created, and who benefits) to the three over-time criteria. Document the judgment.
- Returns and warranties: an assurance-type warranty (guarantee of product conformity) is not a separate performance obligation; a service-type warranty (an additional service) is a separate obligation and needs separate accounting. Estimated refunds/returns create either a liability for expected returns or variable consideration applied per the standard.
- Shipping terms matter: FOB destination vs FOB shipping point affects when control and the risks/rewards transfer and therefore when revenue is recognized.

Required disclosures (brief)
At a minimum, entities should disclose their revenue accounting policy for standard sales, significant judgments (e.g., timing of control transfer), disaggregation of revenue by type or geography if material, contract balances (receivables, contract assets, contract liabilities), and information about remaining performance obligations if material. Practical expedients (e.g., for disclosure of remaining performance obligations) may be available.

Recognizing Standard Revenue: A Practical Guide to ASC 606/IFRS 15 for Straightforward Contracts

What is the standard-revenue case

The “standard-revenue” case refers to contracts that are simple and routine under ASC 606 / IFRS 15: a single promised good or service, a fixed (non-variable) fee, transfer of control at a point in time, no significant financing component, and no material contract modifications. These contracts are common (e.g., sale of a single piece of equipment, a standard service delivered on completion) and generally require straightforward application of the five-step model. This note focuses on practical checks and journal entries that controllers, accountants and finance managers can apply.

Five-step model recap (brief)

1) Identify the contract with a customer.
2) Identify the performance obligations in the contract.
3) Determine the transaction price.
4) Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligation(s).
5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation.

In the standard-revenue case these steps typically map directly to a single promised item: one contract, one performance obligation, transaction price equals the fixed fee, allocation is trivial, and recognition occurs at the point in time when control transfers.

Applying the model to the standard case (detailed)

Step 1 — Contract: Confirm there is a valid, enforceable contract and that collectibility is probable. Practical checks: signed purchase order or sales agreement, evidence of customer acceptance terms, and creditworthiness screening. If collectibility is in doubt, either delay revenue or apply constraining guidance per ASC 606/IFRS 15.

Step 2 — Performance obligations: Verify the contract promises a single good/service. Ask: is the item distinct? Are there implied promises (installation, basic warranty) that are separate? If the contract includes bundled deliverables, consider whether they should be combined or separated for allocation.

Step 3 — Transaction price: For fixed-fee contracts with no variable consideration or significant financing, the transaction price equals the contract price. Confirm there are no embedded discounts, refunds, or contingent rebates. Document why variable consideration and significant financing tests do not apply.

Step 4 — Allocation: With one performance obligation, allocation is trivial (100% to that obligation). With multiple obligations (not the standard case), allocate based on standalone selling prices.

Step 5 — Recognition: Determine whether control transfers over time or at a point in time. For many physical goods, control transfers at delivery or when legal title and risks/rewards pass. Use indicators of control: the customer has legal title, physical possession, accepts the asset, and has the significant risks and rewards. In the standard case, revenue is recognized at a point in time — typically on delivery/acceptance.

Practical documentation: retain a short checklist per contract confirming collectibility assessment, identification of single performance obligation, confirmation no significant financing, and the chosen point of transfer.

Example with numbers and journal entries

Fact pattern: Company A sells a standard machine to Customer B for $50,000. The machine is delivered and accepted on July 15. Cost of goods sold (COGS) is $30,000. No variable consideration, no financing, no post-sale obligations.

Scenario A — Payment on delivery (receipt at same time):
- On delivery and acceptance (recognize revenue):
  Dr Cash 50,000
    Cr Revenue 50,000
  Dr COGS 30,000
    Cr Inventory 30,000

Scenario B — Customer prepaid (received June 1) and delivery July 15:
- On receipt of cash (June 1):
  Dr Cash 50,000
    Cr Contract liability (deferred revenue) 50,000

- On delivery and satisfaction of performance obligation (July 15):
  Dr Contract liability 50,000
    Cr Revenue 50,000
  Dr COGS 30,000
    Cr Inventory 30,000

Notes on presentation and timing: If payment terms imply a significant financing component (e.g., multi-year extended payment), assess whether to adjust the transaction price for the financing effect. For brief prepayments and standard commercial terms, ASC 606/IFRS 15 typically treat this as not significant.

Disclosures: Even in a simple contract, include required disclosures: description of the goods/services, transaction price and timing of revenue recognition, and any significant judgments (e.g., point-of-transfer assessments, collectibility). In the standard case, disclosures are concise but should still indicate that revenue is recognized at a point in time and that no material judgments or estimates were necessary.

Common pitfalls & controls

Common pitfalls
- Ignoring collectibility: treating an obviously at-risk receivable as revenue.
- Overlooking bundled items (installation, training) that might be separate obligations.
- Failing to test for a significant financing component when prepayment or extended payment is present.
- Treating warranties incorrectly: distinguish between assurance-type warranties (part of the performance obligation) and service-type warranties (separate obligation).
- Poor documentation of judgments and approvals.

Suggested controls
- Standard contract review checklist used by sales and revenue accounting before booking revenue.
- Pre-approval of non-standard contract terms (discounts, extended payment, returns) by finance.
- Revenue journal entry templates with required supporting fields (contract ID, customer acceptance evidence, collectibility sign-off).
- Periodic sample audits of new contracts to confirm consistent application.

Quick checklist (one paragraph)

Before recognizing revenue for a standard contract, confirm: valid contract and probable collectibility; single, distinct performance obligation; fixed transaction price with no variable consideration; no significant financing component; clear point-of-transfer evidence (delivery/acceptance). Document each check, obtain required signatures, and use the revenue journal template.

Further reading / sources

Primary authoritative sources: ASC 606 (FASB) and IFRS 15 (IFRS Foundation). Practical guidance and examples: Big Four practice aids (PwC Revenue from Contracts with Customers, Deloitte iGAAP/roadmap, EY revenue guides) and AICPA practice aids. For complex or borderline cases, consult your accounting advisor or external auditor.

Closing / next steps

For routine contracts, apply the five-step model using the checklist above and record revenue at delivery with the simple journal entries shown. For any contract with unusual payment terms, bundled deliverables, variable consideration, or significant financing, escalate to accounting leadership or external advisors for a documented analysis. Title: Standard Revenue Case: A Practical Guide to Revenue Recognition (ASC 606 / IFRS 15)

Hook (lead)
Correct revenue recognition matters: it affects reported profit, KPIs (gross margin, ARR), tax positions, covenant compliance and audit outcomes. ASC 606 and IFRS 15 replace legacy rules with a principles-based, five-step model that focuses on contracts and performance obligations—so getting the basics right for simple sales and common multi-component arrangements avoids restatements and audit queries.

Overview: the five-step model (ASC 606 / IFRS 15)
Both ASC 606 and IFRS 15 require the same five-step approach to recognize revenue from contracts with customers (see ASC 606 guidance summary; IFRS 15 guidance summary):
1. Identify the contract with a customer.
2. Identify the performance obligations (POs) in the contract.
3. Determine the transaction price.
4. Allocate the transaction price to the POs based on relative standalone selling prices.
5. Recognize revenue when (or as) each PO is satisfied (point in time or over time).

This article applies these steps to a standard single-performance-obligation sale and to a common two-component arrangement (product + one-year support). Citations: see FASB ASC 606 overview (ASC 606 guidance summary), IFRS Foundation (IFRS 15 guidance summary), and PwC’s Revenue from Contracts with Customers practical guide for deeper application.

Example 1 — Single performance obligation (goods sale)
Scenario and assumptions (ASC 606 / IFRS 15 application):
- Company A sells a widget on 30 June for $10,000 (invoice, 30-day credit). The customer takes control on delivery on 30 June. No other promises (no returns, no discounts). Cost of goods sold (COGS) = $6,000.

Step application:
- Step 1: Contract exists (commercial substance, enforceable rights, collectibility expected).
- Step 2: Single PO: transfer of the widget.
- Step 3: Transaction price = $10,000 (fixed, no variable consideration).
- Step 4: Allocation not needed (single PO).
- Step 5: Recognize revenue at point in time when control transfers (delivery on 30 June).

Journal entries (ASC 606 / IFRS 15 treatment):
On delivery (30 June):
- Dr Accounts receivable 10,000
- Cr Revenue 10,000
- Dr Cost of goods sold 6,000
- Cr Inventory 6,000

If the customer had prepaid on 15 June, the initial entry would be:
- Dr Cash 10,000
- Cr Contract liability (deferred revenue) 10,000
Then on delivery (30 June):
- Dr Contract liability 10,000
- Cr Revenue 10,000

Key point: recognition timing follows transfer of control (not necessarily invoice or cash receipt). Document your control indicators (legal title, physical possession, significant risks/rewards, customer acceptance).

Example 2 — Two-component arrangement: product + one-year support
Scenario and assumptions (explicit judgments labeled):
- Company B sells a machine and a 12-month support package for a single contract price of $9,000 on 1 July. Standalone selling prices (SSP) are: machine $8,000; 12-month support $1,200 (i.e., $100/month). There are no other promises. Assume collectibility is probable and there’s no significant financing component.

Step application and allocation (ASC 606 / IFRS 15):
- Step 1: Contract exists.
- Step 2: Identify two distinct POs: (A) machine (transfer of control at delivery) and (B) support (series of services over 12 months).
- Step 3: Transaction price = $9,000.
- Step 4: Allocate price by relative SSPs.

Allocation calculation (plain-text table):
Total SSP = 8,000 (machine) + 1,200 (support) = 9,200
- Machine allocation = 9,000 * (8,000 / 9,200) = 7,826.09
- Support allocation = 9,000 * (1,200 / 9,200) = 1,173.91

(Table: Allocation calculation)
- Machine SSP: 8,000 — Allocated revenue: 7,826.09
- Support SSP: 1,200 — Allocated revenue: 1,173.91
- Total contract price: 9,000

Recognition timing and journal entries (ASC 606 / IFRS 15):
On delivery (1 July):
- Recognize machine revenue immediately: 7,826.09
- Recognize a contract liability for the support portion: 1,173.91 (deferred revenue to be recognized over time)

Entry on 1 July:
- Dr Accounts receivable (or Cash) 9,000
- Cr Revenue (machine) 7,826.09
- Cr Contract liability (support) 1,173.91

Monthly recognition of support revenue (1 July–30 June next year):
- Monthly revenue = 1,173.91 / 12 ≈ 97.82 per month (label assumptions: rounding differences accepted)
Each month:
- Dr Contract liability 97.82
- Cr Revenue (support) 97.82

If costs for support are incurred monthly, also record those as COGS or service expense as incurred. Document SSP determination (observable prices preferred; if not observable, use an estimate consistent with the standard).

Common pitfalls & internal controls (practical checks)
- Variable consideration: discounts, rebates, returns and performance bonuses require estimation (constrain if significant uncertainty). Maintain policies and historical data for judgement.
- Contract modifications: treat as separate contract or modification; update allocation and revenue prospective/retrospective per guidance.
- Collectibility: if not probable, account as a liability until performance and payment assurance improve.
- Significant financing component: if payment timing gives a material financing benefit, separate interest from revenue (rare for typical short-term sales, but check when payment terms exceed one year or large upfront/long-tail arrangements).
- Principal vs agent: determine whether you control the good/service before transfer (principal recognizes gross revenue; agent recognizes net fee).
- Disclosures: ensure you can disclose disaggregated revenue, contract liabilities, significant judgements, and remaining performance obligations as required by ASC 606/IFRS 15.
Controls to implement:
- Standard contract worksheet template mapping the five steps.
- SSP schedules and supporting evidence for bundle allocations.
- Monthly review of contract liabilities and deferred revenue roll-forwards.

Quick practitioner checklist (6–8 items)
1. Do you have a signed contract or equivalent evidence of an enforceable arrangement? (Step 1)
2. Have you identified and documented each performance obligation? (Step 2)
3. Is the transaction price fixed or does variable consideration apply? Document estimates and constraints. (Step 3)
4. Do you have standalone selling prices or a consistent method to estimate them? Prepare allocation calculations. (Step 4)
5. Determine when control transfers for each PO—point in time or over time—and record timing-based journal entries. (Step 5)
6. Check for significant financing, principal vs agent, collectibility issues, and contract modifications.
7. Reconcile contract liabilities and revenue recognized each period; keep supporting schedules for auditors.
8. Ensure disclosures are complete (disaggregation, RPOs, significant judgements).

When to escalate / seek specialist advice
Escalate to technical accounting when you have material variable consideration, complex bundled arrangements without observable SSPs, significant contract modifications, or long-term financing aspects. For public companies, consider SEC interpretive guidance where relevant.

Sources and further reading
- FASB ASC 606 guidance summary: https://asc.fasb.org (search ASC 606 overview)
- IFRS 15 guidance summary: https://www.ifrs.org (search IFRS 15 revenue from contracts with customers)
- PwC: Revenue from Contracts with Customers (practical guide): https://www.pwc.com/us/en/cfodirect/publications/accounting-guides/revenue-from-contracts-with-customers.html

Call to action
Use the attached worksheet template to map new contracts to the five steps. For material or judgement-heavy arrangements, prepare a concise memo documenting assumptions (SSPs, variability, collectibility) for audit review.

Title: Recognizing Revenue for a Standard Sale of Goods under ASC 606 / IFRS 15

Summary
This practical guide explains when and how to recognize revenue for a typical sale of goods where a single performance obligation is satisfied at a point in time. It covers the five-step model, indicators that control has transferred, treatment of prepayments and sales tax, journal entries for common events, a worked numeric example, disclosure and presentation implications, a brief contrast with over-time recognition, and a short compliance checklist for reviewers.

Core principle and the five-step model
ASC 606 and IFRS 15 center on a control-based principle: an entity recognizes revenue when it transfers control of promised goods or services to a customer for an amount that reflects the consideration it expects to receive. Apply the five-step model:
1) Identify the contract with the customer.
2) Identify the performance obligations in the contract (promises to transfer goods or services).
3) Determine the transaction price.
4) Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations.
5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies each performance obligation.

Why most standard product sales are point-in-time
Most routine product sales involve a single performance obligation satisfied at a point in time because control of the goods typically transfers on delivery. Indicators that control has transferred include: transfer of legal title, transfer of physical possession, transfer of significant risks and rewards, customer acceptance, and the seller's present right to payment. Not all indicators must be present, but the entity should consider all relevant facts and circumstances and document its judgment.

Prepayments and deposits
When a customer prepays (deposit), the seller has received consideration but has not yet satisfied the performance obligation. Under ASC 606 / IFRS 15, the appropriate accounting is:
- Dr Cash
- Cr Contract liability (deferred revenue)

The contract liability remains on the balance sheet until the performance obligation is satisfied, at which time the liability is derecognized and revenue is recognized.

Sales tax
Amounts collected on behalf of tax authorities (sales tax, VAT, GST) are not revenue. Record them as liabilities: Dr Cash; Cr Sales tax/VAT payable. Do not include sales tax in transaction price or in revenue unless the tax is borne by the seller (rare for sales tax/VAT).

Common journal entries (typical events)
1) Sale on delivery (no prepayment)
- On delivery and invoicing:
  Dr Accounts receivable (or Cash)
  Cr Revenue
  Dr Cost of goods sold
  Cr Inventory
- Sales tax collected (if applicable):
  Dr Cash/AR
  Cr Sales tax payable
  (and separate Cr Revenue for the price exclusive of tax)

2) Sale with prepayment (deposit)
- On receipt of prepayment:
  Dr Cash
  Cr Contract liability (deferred revenue)
- On delivery (performance obligation satisfied):
  Dr Contract liability
  Cr Revenue
  Dr Cost of goods sold
  Cr Inventory

3) Sales tax collected (separate entry)
- At receipt/invoice:
  Dr Cash/AR
  Cr Sales tax payable
  (Revenue entry reflects amount exclusive of tax)

Worked numeric example
Facts: Contract price = $10,000; seller's cost = $6,000. Customer prepays $10,000 on Jan 1. Seller delivers and transfers control on Jan 15. Sales tax = 0 (handled separately if present).

Journal entries:
- Jan 1 (receipt of prepayment):
  Dr Cash 10,000
  Cr Contract liability (deferred revenue) 10,000

- Jan 15 (on delivery; performance obligation satisfied):
  Dr Contract liability 10,000
  Cr Revenue 10,000
  Dr Cost of goods sold 6,000
  Cr Inventory 6,000

P&L and balance sheet impact (after delivery):
- Income statement: Revenue $10,000; COGS $6,000; Gross profit $4,000.
- Balance sheet: Contract liability cleared (0 for this transaction); inventory reduced by $6,000; cash increased by $10,000 (from Jan 1). Net equity increases by $4,000 (profit), subject to tax and other items.

Disclosure and financial statement presentation
- Presentation: Revenue appears in the income statement (often by major product line). Contract liabilities (deferred revenue) appear on the balance sheet as a current or non-current liability depending on expected timing of satisfaction. If the seller has a right to consideration before transfer and expects to satisfy the obligation within the normal operating cycle, the liability is typically current.
- Disclosures: ASC 606 / IFRS 15 require narrative and quantitative disclosures about contracts with customers, including a reconciliation of contract liabilities, significant judgments about timing of satisfaction of performance obligations, and information about remaining performance obligations when material. For standard sales, a short explanation that revenue is recognized at a point in time upon transfer of control and the nature of the evidence supporting that conclusion is usually sufficient. Also disclose contract liabilities and changes during the period.
- Note on variable consideration: Not relevant in this standard fixed-price example, but entities must consider variable consideration when present and apply constraint guidance.

Brief contrast: over-time recognition
Some contracts are satisfied over time (e.g., construction, long-term services). Revenue is recognized over time when any of these criteria are met: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits, the customer controls the asset being created, or the seller has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date and costs incurred have no alternative use. The distinguishing factor is continued transfer of control over time rather than at a single point.

Common pitfalls and compliance checklist
- Pitfalls:
  * Treating deposits/prepayments as revenue before transfer of control.
  * Ignoring indicators of control (e.g., acceptance clauses, title retention).
  * Misclassifying sales taxes as revenue.
  * Failing to identify distinct performance obligations (e.g., bundled goods/services).
  * Inadequate disclosure of significant judgments (timing of recognition, contract liabilities).

- Practical checklist for reviewers/clients:
  1) Have you applied the five-step model and documented the judgment on timing of control transfer? 
  2) Is any consideration variable or contingent (not a standard case)? If yes, apply variable consideration guidance.
  3) Are deposits/prepayments recorded as contract liabilities until delivery? 
  4) Are sales taxes separated from revenue and recorded as liabilities? 
  5) Are disclosures sufficient about significant judgments, contract liabilities, and revenue recognized in the period?

Authoritative sources and further reading
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers — https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ifrs-15-revenue-from-contracts-with-customers/
- FASB ASC 606 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) — https://asc.fasb.org (search ASC 606)

- Deloitte: Revenue recognition roadmaps and guides — https://www2.deloitte.com
- KPMG: Revenue insights — https://home.kpmg
- AICPA: Practical implementation tools and illustrations — https://www.aicpa.org

What is a standard revenue case?

A “standard‑revenue case” describes a straightforward, predictable revenue stream in which pricing, deliverables, and timing of customer satisfaction are clear. Typical examples include fixed monthly subscriptions, one‑time product sales under a standard returns policy, or other transactions with limited contingencies or variable elements. These cases tend to have a single performance obligation (or clearly separable obligations), a fixed or readily estimable transaction price, and predictable timing of revenue recognition.

Why this distinction matters

Classifying a revenue stream as standard simplifies forecasting, reporting, and internal controls. Standard cases reduce judgment in revenue recognition, lower audit risk, and make unit economics easier to compute and monitor (ARR, ARPU, CAC payback). Conversely, nonstandard or complex revenue—characterized by material variable consideration, complex bundling, or frequent contract modifications—requires more judgment under ASC 606 / IFRS 15 and complicates forecasting and controls.

Accounting principles (high level)

Under the principles of ASC 606 and IFRS 15, the core steps are: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate the price to performance obligations, and recognize revenue when (or as) obligations are satisfied. In practice for standard revenue:

- If there is a single, ongoing service (e.g., monthly SaaS), revenue is typically recognized over time, ratably across the subscription period.
- If the sale transfers control of a distinct good with no remaining obligations (e.g., a one‑time product), revenue is generally recognized at a point in time (the sale date).
- Variable consideration (discounts, rebates, refunds, usage fees) requires estimate and may prevent straightforward recognition until sufficient history or constraints reduce risk.

Sources: FASB ASC 606 and IFRS 15 summaries provide the authoritative framework (see FASB ASC 606 summary: https://www.fasb.org and IFRS 15 overview: https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ifrs-15-revenue-from-contracts-with-customers/). For practical guidance on identifying performance obligations and variable consideration, see guidance from Big Four firms (e.g., PwC and Deloitte summaries: https://www.pwc.com and https://www2.deloitte.com).

How to tell if your revenue is standard: a short checklist

- Fixed price or predictable fee schedule (no meaningful variable consideration)
- Single performance obligation or clearly separable deliverables
- Predictable timing of satisfaction (e.g., monthly subscription coverage or on‑delivery product sales)
- Minimal or estimable returns, rebates, or credits
- Few contract modifications or financing components

If you tick most boxes, you likely have a standard‑revenue case. If not, treat it as complex and involve accounting/finance early.

Forecasting implications

Standard revenue supports simpler, reliable forecasting: cohort‑based models, steady cash‑flow projections, and easier scenario analysis. For subscriptions, MRR/ARR cohort curves and retention cohorts can be projected with fewer variables. For one‑time sales, historical seasonality and sales pipeline conversion rates usually suffice. Complex arrangements—usage billing, significant variable consideration, or bundles with uncertain separability—require probabilistic scenarios and close collaboration with accounting to reflect revenue recognition timing.

Practical examples

1) SaaS monthly subscription (standard)
Most SaaS with a fixed monthly fee and a single service obligation is a textbook standard case. The transaction price is fixed; performance is continuous across the month; revenue is recognized ratably over the subscription term. This yields stable MRR/ARR metrics and straightforward churn analysis. Practitioner resources on SaaS metrics can help operationalize tracking (see Point Nine and Bessemer for SaaS metric frameworks: https://www.pointnine.com/blog/saas-metrics/ and https://www.bvp.com/atlas).

2) One‑time product sale with returns window (often standard)
A physical product sold with a standard returns policy can still be standard if returns are historically low and can be reasonably estimated. Recognize revenue at the point control transfers (sale), but record an allowance for expected returns. If returns are volatile or significant, the case becomes less standard and requires more conservative recognition.

3) Bundled product + paid installation (borderline)
If a product is sold with optional paid installation, the arrangement may remain standard when the deliverables are separable and each has a distinct standalone selling price. Allocate the transaction price and recognize revenue for each obligation when satisfied (product at delivery; installation over or at completion). If the bundle’s elements are highly interdependent or installation includes ongoing obligations, classification becomes nonstandard and needs deeper accounting analysis.

When a case is NOT standard

Common triggers that push you into complex revenue territory:
- Material variable consideration (usage‑based fees, significant rebates, or large refunds)
- Complex bundling where separability is unclear
- Significant financing components (long‑dated payment terms affecting price)
- Frequent contract modifications or bespoke terms
- High judgment in estimating returns, discounts, or performance outcomes

Metrics to report for standard revenue streams

For standard streams, emphasize clarity and comparability with these metrics:
- ARR / MRR and NRR (Net Revenue Retention)
- MRR churn and customer churn
- ARPU (Average Revenue Per User)
- Gross margin on revenue recognized
- Billing lag days (days between invoice and recognized revenue if relevant)

Checklist and recommended next steps for product and finance teams

Data to collect
- Contract templates and common variations
- Historical returns, rebates, and refund rates
- Usage patterns (if applicable) and billing records
- Timing of delivery and invoicing

Controls to implement
- Standardized contract language and approval workflow
- Clear records of performance obligations and start/end dates
- Allowances and estimation methodologies documented and reviewed periodically
- Reconciliation between billing, GL, and recognized revenue

Who to involve
- FP&A for forecasting and metrics
- Accounting for revenue recognition and policy decisions
- Legal for contract language and change control
- Audit/internal controls for periodic reviews

Caveats and final note

This article is meant to guide classification and internal practice; it is not a substitute for professional accounting or legal advice. For borderline or complex revenue arrangements, consult your accounting team or external auditors for formal guidance.

Selected resources

- FASB ASC 606 summary: https://www.fasb.org
- IFRS 15: https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ifrs-15-revenue-from-contracts-with-customers/
- PwC revenue recognition resources: https://www.pwc.com
- Deloitte ASC 606 overview: https://www2.deloitte.com
- SaaS metric primers: Point Nine (https://www.pointnine.com/blog/saas-metrics/), Bessemer/BVP (https://www.bvp.com/atlas)

Rationale: Clear, audience‑focused draft covering definition, accounting and forecasting implications, practical examples, checklist, and next steps — ready for editorial review.
